Based on the sources I was able to access, here is the verse-by-verse commentary:

## Leviticus 14:1-28 — Verse-by-Verse Notes

### v. 1: "Then the LORD said to Moses"
The standard introductory formula found 28 times in Leviticus, underscoring that these instructions carry divine authority, not human invention. Moses alone received this particular revelation (not Moses and Aaron jointly, as in some other passages). Precept Austin notes this refrain echoes throughout the book as a marker of Mosaic authorship. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_14_commentary; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-14/)

### v. 2: "This is the law for the one afflicted with a skin disease on the day of his cleansing, when he is brought to the priest."
This "law" (Hebrew *torah*) is a prescription for ceremonial cleansing, not a medical cure. MacArthur stresses that this law was "not for healing from leprosy…but rather for the ceremonial cleansing, which needed to be performed after the person was declared clean" (cited at https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_14_commentary). Gill notes the rabbinic tradition (Jarchi) that purification could not be performed at night. "He shall be brought to the priest" — the leper could not simply walk into the camp; he had to be presented near the camp boundary for the priest to come out. Typologically, Gill sees the priest as a type of Christ, to whom "leprous sinners must be brought for cleansing." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/14.htm; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-14/)

### v. 3: "The priest is to go outside the camp to examine him…"
The priest went *out* to the leper — the leper did not come to the tabernacle. Keil & Delitzsch explain that the leper had been excluded from the covenant nation, regarded as one under the "ban of death," so the priest had to go to him. Guzik (Enduring Word) draws a typological parallel: just as Jesus went "outside the camp" (Hebrews 13:11-13) to reach the unclean, so the priest went outside to meet the healed leper. If the disease had healed (literally, "healed away from" him), the ritual could proceed. Note: healing preceded cleansing; the ceremony did not cause healing. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-14/; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/leviticus-14.html)

### v. 4: "Two live clean birds, cedar wood, scarlet yarn, and hyssop"
These items formed the first-stage ritual outside the camp. No specific bird species is mandated — Gill notes they simply had to be clean (per Leviticus 11) and alive (not shot or maimed). Rabbinic tradition (Mishnah Negaim) added that the two birds should match in appearance, size, and value.

**Cedar wood**: Keil & Delitzsch say cedar was chosen for its antiseptic, rot-resistant qualities — a "symbol of the continuance of life." Guzik notes cedar is "extremely resistant to disease and rot." Gill adds that cedar, as the highest of trees, could represent the pride that leprosy sometimes punished (Miriam, Uzziah), but evangelically it pictures Christ's incorruption and the durable efficacy of His death. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/14.htm)

**Scarlet**: Most commentators (Rooker, cited by Guzik) believe this is scarlet yarn or thread, not cloth. Keil & Delitzsch call it "coccus" — scarlet wool, "a symbol of freshness of life, or fulness of vital energy." Gill notes scarlet dye came from a worm (the cochineal insect), making it a picture of both the blood of Christ and the humility proper to a cleansed sinner. Benson says it represents "both the leper's sinfulness, and the blood of Christ, and the happy change of the leper's colour and complexion." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-14/; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/leviticus-14.html)

**Hyssop**: A small, brush-like plant used for sprinkling blood or water (Exodus 12:22; Numbers 19:18). Keil & Delitzsch call it a symbol of "purification from the corruption of death." Guzik notes David's cry "purge me with hyssop" (Psalm 51:7) meant David identified himself as being as bad as a leper — but a cleansed one. Precept Austin cites Today in the Word noting that the exact botanical identity of biblical hyssop is debated; it may be a caper plant or an herb from the basil family. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-14/; https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_14_commentary)

### v. 5: "One of the birds be slaughtered over fresh water in a clay pot"
The bird was killed *over* an earthenware vessel containing "living water" (Hebrew *mayim chayyim*), i.e., water from a flowing spring or brook — not stagnant cistern water. The blood dripped into the water and mixed with it. Keil & Delitzsch explain: "slain in such a manner that its blood should flow into the fresh water which was in a vessel, and should mix with it." The earthen vessel was cheap and disposable. Gill sees Christological typology: the earthen vessel represents Christ's humanity (cf. 2 Corinthians 4:7), and the running water mixed with blood pictures the water and blood from Christ's pierced side (John 19:34), signifying both sanctification and justification. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/leviticus-14.html; https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/14.htm)

### v. 6: "Dip the live bird together with the cedar wood, scarlet yarn, and hyssop into the blood"
The living bird, along with the cedar stick, scarlet thread, and hyssop branch, was dipped into the blood-and-water mixture in the clay pot. Clarke describes how these items were assembled: "The cedar-wood served for the handle, the hyssop and living bird were attached to it by means of the scarlet wool or crimson fillet. The bird was so bound to this handle as that its tail should be downwards, in order to be dipped into the blood." This created a sprinkling instrument (aspergillum). Rabbinic debate (cited by Gill) exists over whether the living bird was bundled with the other items or held separately. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-14/; https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/14.htm)

### v. 7: "Seven times he shall sprinkle…Then he shall pronounce him clean and release the live bird into the open field"
Seven-fold sprinkling signifies complete purification (seven being the number of covenant and completeness). After sprinkling, the priest declared the person clean. Then the blood-stained living bird was released to fly away into the open country.

**Interpretations of the two birds differ somewhat across traditions:**

- **Christological/typological (Gill, Guzik, Gaebelein, Coffman, Benson):** The slain bird pictures Christ's death; the living bird, marked with sacrificial blood and released heavenward, pictures Christ's resurrection (and ascension). Guzik adds it also pictures the cleansed sinner "resurrected and free in the resurrected Jesus Christ." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-14/)

- **Keil & Delitzsch (Lutheran/conservative):** Both birds symbolise the leper himself. The slain bird shows that the leper *would have* died for his uncleanness if God had not mercifully delivered him. The living bird, bathed in blood and water and released, represents the leper's deliverance from the ban of death and his restoration to freedom and community. The birds were chosen because their free, rapid flight best pictures "free unfettered movement in all directions." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/leviticus-14.html)

- **Clarke (Methodist):** Calls the released bird "the scape-bird" and compares the rite to the scapegoat of Leviticus 16 — the living bird carries away pollution symbolically. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-14/)

- **Peake's Commentary (modern scholarship):** Suggests that the ritual elements — dipping, releasing a bird, shaving hair — "had very possibly an original connexion with what would now be called magic — getting rid of the spirit or demon of disease." However, Coffman forcefully rejects this view, noting that healing preceded the ritual, so no magical efficacy was attributed to it. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/leviticus-14.html; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/leviticus-14.html)

### v. 8: "Wash his clothes, shave off all his hair, and bathe with water…he may enter the camp, but he must remain outside his tent for seven days"
After the bird ritual, the cleansed person underwent bodily cleansing: washing clothes, shaving all body hair, bathing. He could now enter the camp but had to live outside his own tent for seven days. Poole (cited by Guzik) gives three reasons for the shaving: to demonstrate perfect soundness of the skin, to remove any residual disease particles from hair or clothes, and to teach him "to put off his old lusts, and become a new man." Guzik notes the public nature of living outside one's tent proved to the community that healing was genuine. Keil & Delitzsch, citing the Chaldee paraphrase, say the seven-day separation from the tent also meant abstaining from conjugal relations, "that he might not defile himself again." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-14/; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/leviticus-14.html)

### v. 9: "On the seventh day he must shave off all his hair…his beard, his eyebrows…"
A second complete shaving, even more thorough — specifying head, beard, and eyebrows. This, with washing, completed the second-stage purification. Guzik observes that the recovered leper "would start all over again as if he was a newborn baby — as if he was born again." Gill notes that Mishnaic tradition held that if even two hairs remained, the shaving was invalid. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-14/; https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/14.htm)

### v. 10: "On the eighth day he is to bring two unblemished male lambs, an unblemished ewe lamb a year old, a grain offering…and one log of olive oil"
The eighth day marked the third and final stage — at the tabernacle. Three lambs: two males (one guilt/trespass offering, one burnt offering) and one female yearling (sin offering). The grain offering was "three-tenths of an ephah" of fine flour mixed with oil — a substantial amount (Guzik estimates between 5 and 20 pounds). The "log" of oil was about 10 ounces or one-third of a liter. This was an expensive requirement. Keil & Delitzsch note that the larger-than-normal grain offering represented "diligence in good works." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-14/; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/leviticus-14.html)

### v. 11: "The priest who performs the cleansing shall present the one to be cleansed…before the LORD at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting"
The movement traces full restoration: from outside the camp (v. 3), to inside the camp (v. 8), to the very entrance of the Tent of Meeting (v. 11). Rooker (quoted by Guzik) says this progression is "another way of describing the cleansed man's full restoration." Guzik adds that the priest "made" the leper clean only in the declarative sense — by applying God's revealed word to judge the person's condition. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-14/)

### vv. 12-13: "The priest is to take one of the male lambs and present it as a guilt offering…wave them as a wave offering…slaughter the lamb in the sanctuary area"
The first male lamb was a guilt/trespass offering (*asham*). Uniquely for a guilt offering, it was "waved" before the LORD along with the log of oil. Keil & Delitzsch explain that waving transferred the lamb and oil symbolically to the Lord, representing the offerer's dedication to God's service — similar to the Levites' consecration (Numbers 8:11, 15). The guilt offering was required (they argue) because the leper's exclusion from the covenant nation had cost him his covenant rights; restoration required a consecration-offering. A minority view (cited but not endorsed by Keil & Delitzsch: Riehm, Oehler) regarded it as a *mulcta* (penalty) for the theocratical duties the leper had failed to perform during his illness. The meat belonged to the priest; it was "most holy." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/leviticus-14.html; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-14/)

### v. 14: "Put some of the blood…on the right earlobe…thumb of his right hand…big toe of his right foot"
This blood application was a dramatic departure from the normal guilt offering ritual. It mirrored the consecration of priests (Leviticus 8:22-24). Guzik explains the symbolism: blood on the right ear = "this one should hear God first"; right thumb = "this one should put his hand to do God's will first"; right big toe = "this one should follow God's path first." Keil & Delitzsch similarly state: the organ of hearing, and the members used in acting and walking according to God's commandments, were "sanctified through the power of the atoning blood." Trapp (quoted by Guzik): "To signify that all Christ's sanctified ones have a hearing ear, an active hand, a nimble foot to walk in the way that is called holy." Dummelow adds that this anointing signified "reconsecration to the service of God, and the readmission of the leper to the privileges of the tabernacle." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-14/; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/leviticus-14.html; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcb/leviticus-14.html)

### vv. 15-16: "The priest shall take some of the log of olive oil, pour it into his left palm, dip his right forefinger…sprinkle some of the oil…seven times before the LORD"
Oil was poured into the priest's left palm; he dipped his right forefinger and sprinkled oil seven times "before the LORD" — that is, toward the altar, not on the person. Keil & Delitzsch say this consecrated the oil to God and sanctified it for the subsequent anointing. Guzik provides an extended meditation on oil as a symbol of the Holy Spirit: oil heals, lights, warms, invigorates, adorns, polishes, and lubricates — seven functions, each reflecting the Spirit's work in the believer. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-14/; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/leviticus-14.html)

### v. 17: "Put some of the oil…on the right earlobe…thumb…big toe…on top of the blood of the guilt offering"
The oil was applied to the same three places as the blood — ear, thumb, toe — and specifically *on top of* (superimposed upon) the blood. The sequence is theologically significant: the anointing of oil (Spirit) rests upon the foundation of the blood sacrifice. Guzik: "The anointing of the Holy Spirit could not come unless it was upon the work of a blood sacrifice." Keil & Delitzsch contrast this with priestly consecration: priests received blood on ear, thumb, and toe but *not* oil on those same spots. This unique addition signified that everything the restored leper heard, did, and walked should be under the anointing of the Holy Spirit. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-14/; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/leviticus-14.html)

### v. 18: "The rest of the oil…put on the head of the one to be cleansed, to make atonement for him before the LORD"
The remaining oil was poured on the head — an anointing akin to that of priests and kings. Guzik: "This dramatic act said to the leper, 'There is a sense in which God regards you as a king and a priest.'" Keil & Delitzsch explain that the oil poured on the head represented the Spirit of life the leper had received from God, now fully appropriated to his person. This action "made atonement" — the oil anointing sealed the reconciliation and reinstatement into covenant privileges. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-14/; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/leviticus-14.html)

### vv. 19-20: "The priest is to sacrifice the sin offering…slaughter the burnt offering and offer it on the altar, with the grain offering…and he will be clean"
After the guilt offering and oil anointing, the sin offering (the ewe lamb) expiated the uncleanness itself, then the burnt offering and grain offering expressed the restored worshipper's total dedication and devotion to God. Rooker (cited by Guzik): "The sin offering would put an individual in good standing with God, while the burnt offering and grain offering symbolized the renewed dedication of the worshiper and of his devotion to God." Keil & Delitzsch frame it as: the trespass-offering restored covenant rights; the sin-offering cleansed the residual sin that had manifested in the leprosy; the burnt and grain offerings "embodied the sanctification of all his members to the service of the Lord."

Guzik notes the striking fact that there is no Old Testament record of an Israelite leper being restored through this ritual (apart from Miriam in Numbers 12). Fructhenbaum (cited by Precept Austin) notes that the rabbis classified the healing of a Jewish leper as a "messianic miracle" — one reserved for the Messiah alone — since no Jew had ever been healed of leprosy from the giving of the Law until Jesus. This explains the stir when Jesus healed lepers and sent them to the priests (Luke 5:12-14). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-14/; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/leviticus-14.html; https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_14_commentary)

### vv. 21-22: "If, however, the person is poor and cannot afford these offerings…"
A gracious provision for poverty. Instead of three lambs, the poor person brought only one male lamb (for the guilt offering — this could not be reduced) plus two turtledoves or pigeons (one for sin offering, one for burnt offering) and a reduced grain offering (one-tenth ephah instead of three-tenths). Keil & Delitzsch stress that "no diminution was allowed in the trespass-offering as the consecration-offering, since this was the *conditio sine qua non* of reinstatement in full covenant rights." Gill notes this mirrors the provision in Leviticus 5:11 and 12:8. Guzik observes that most lepers were likely poor — the disease isolated them from economic life — so God's accommodation was both merciful and practical. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-14/; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/leviticus-14.html)

### v. 23: "On the eighth day he is to bring them for his cleansing to the priest at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting before the LORD"
The poor person came to the same place, before the same priest, and before the same LORD. There was no second-class status in God's presence. Guzik emphasises this: "The poor man brought his offering to the same place, in the same manner, and to the same priests as the richer man." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-14/)

### vv. 24-25: "The priest shall take the lamb for the guilt offering, along with the log of olive oil, and wave them…put some of the blood…on the right earlobe…thumb…big toe"
The guilt offering ritual for the poor was identical to that for the wealthy (vv. 12-14). The waving, slaughter, and blood application to ear, thumb, and toe were all repeated without reduction. The guilt offering was the irreducible core. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-14/)

### vv. 26-28: "The priest is to pour some of the oil into his left palm…sprinkle…seven times…put some of the oil…on the right earlobe…thumb…big toe—on the same places as the blood"
The oil ritual for the poor man is identical to vv. 15-17. Oil in the left palm, right-finger sprinkling seven times before the LORD, then application to ear, thumb, and toe *upon the blood*. The phrase "on the same places as the blood of the guilt offering" (v. 28) reinforces that the oil (symbolising the Holy Spirit) always rests on the foundation of shed blood. Guzik: "Oil has a consistent association with the Holy Spirit in the Bible." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-14/)

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ

No sharp confessional divide emerged in the sources accessed for this passage. The primary difference lies in *emphasis* and *hermeneutical approach*, not contradictory interpretation:

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word/David Guzik):** Strong emphasis on the Holy Spirit typology in the oil anointing. Guzik devotes extended space to seven functions of oil mirroring the Spirit's work (heals, lights, warms, invigorates, adorns, polishes, lubricates). The cleansed leper's ear, thumb, and toe anointing "has special relevance as a picture of what God does for those restored from their leprous-like sin in the New Covenant," tied to Ezekiel 36:27's promise of the Spirit's outpouring. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-14/)

**Baptist/Reformed (Gill):** Strongly Christological throughout. Gill finds Christ in every element: the two birds = Christ's two natures or two estates (humiliation and exaltation); the cedar = Christ's incorruption; the scarlet = Christ's bloody sufferings; the hyssop = the purgative nature of His blood. Also engages heavily with rabbinic sources (Mishnah, Jarchi, Ben Gersom, Maimonides), reflecting the Baptist scholarly tradition of engaging Jewish sources. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/14.htm)

**Lutheran (Keil & Delitzsch):** The most theologically and symbolically precise reading. Keil & Delitzsch carefully distinguish between what the rite *did* and *did not* do: the first bird was not a true sacrifice (no altar, no sprinkling of blood on an altar) but a symbolic representation that the leper *would have* died but for God's mercy. They also carefully explain why a *guilt* offering was required (restoration of lost covenant rights), rejecting the minority "penalty" view. The oil represents "the spirit of life" the leper received from God, which is then sanctified and applied. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/leviticus-14.html)

**Methodist/Wesleyan (Benson, Clarke):** Benson draws a clean Christological typology: the slain bird = Christ dying; the living bird = Christ rising. Clarke gives a very practical description of how the sprinkling instrument was physically assembled and draws the parallel to the scapegoat. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/leviticus-14.html)

## Other Views

**Modern Scholarship (Peake's Commentary):** Peake raises several critical observations:
- The two-bird ritual, the releasing of the bird (cf. the Azazel goat, Leviticus 16), and the shaving of hair "all suggest ideas which had very possibly an original connexion with what would now be called magic — getting rid of the spirit or demon of disease."
- The guilt offering is puzzling: there is no suggestion of the extra fifth required in Leviticus 5-6, and the ritual differs (oil is used, the whole offering is waved). Peake suggests it "is called a guilt offering, because, as additional to the sin and burnt offerings, it could be called nothing else."
- "Even 'atonement' (v. 19), though there is of course no actual 'sin,' is necessary, because rites like these alone can secure power to join again in the *communio sacrorum*."
- Peake questions whether true leprosy (Hansen's disease) alone was in view: "If true leprosy alone had been intended, apart from eczema or skin-disease, the rite could hardly ever have been needed." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/leviticus-14.html)

**Coffman's Rebuttal (Church of Christ/Conservative):** Coffman directly rejects the "magical origins" theory: "The error in such a view is manifest in the fact that the leper in this chapter had to be healed FIRST, before any of the ceremonies here mentioned could begin. No efficacy whatever to heal the victim is implied or attributed to the ceremonies." He also notes Wenham's observation that "Israel differed from her neighbors, who went in for exorcism and magical attempts to cure disease. In Israel, a man had to seek help directly from God in prayer." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/leviticus-14.html)

**Catholic and Orthodox Readings:** Unfortunately, I was unable to retrieve specific Catholic (newadvent.org, catholic.com) or Orthodox (oca.org) commentary pages for Leviticus 14 within the search and fetch limits. These would typically emphasise the typological connection to the sacraments (anointing with oil prefiguring the anointing of the sick, the blood and water prefiguring the Eucharist and Baptism) and read the passage within the Church's liturgical and patristic tradition.

**Debated Modern Teaching (Prosperity/Word of Faith/Hyper-Grace):** No search results from the permitted sites addressed prosperity, Word of Faith, or hyper-grace interpretations of Leviticus 14 specifically. These movements typically draw more directly on New Testament healing narratives and Abrahamic covenant passages than on Levitical purification law.
